title: The Extra Key
summary: An attacker got a foothold through a web account and made themselves at home: a new administrator account and a hidden way to become root on demand. Find both and shut them out.
story: You run app1, a Linux web server for {{CO}} (made up), on 10.10.7.0/24. Monitoring flagged an odd login overnight. You have a root console on app1. Nothing has been cleaned up yet.
goal: Identify the account the attacker used, the extra administrator they created and the hidden set-user-ID backdoor they left, capture the flag they dropped, then remove both footholds - before their backdoor is used to wire in permanent root.
skills: auth logs, listing users and groups, finding set-user-ID files, removing a user, cleaning up

flags.name: The flag in the attacker's dropped note

questions.ask: Which existing account did the attacker sign in with?
questions.explain: The web service account appears in /var/log/secure, signed in from the attacker's address.

questions.ask: What extra administrator account did they create?
questions.explain: A new user in the wheel group that you did not create - compare /etc/passwd and the wheel group.

questions.ask: What is the full path of the hidden set-user-ID backdoor?
questions.explain: find / -perm -4000 lists set-user-ID files; one with a hidden name is a root-owned copy of a shell.

attacker.run: echo '{{ROGUE}} ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' > /etc/sudoers.d/{{ROGUE}} 2>/dev/null; chmod 440 /etc/sudoers.d/{{ROGUE}} 2>/dev/null; true
attacker.note: The backdoor account was still there, so the attacker wired in permanent passwordless root for it.

hints.text: Start with the sign-in log: grep -Ei 'accepted|failed' /var/log/secure. One of the service accounts signed in from an outside address. Note the account name and the address.

Attackers often add their own account. List the people who can log in (cut -d: -f1,3,7 /etc/passwd) and who can become root (getent group wheel). An account you did not create, sitting in wheel, is the attacker's. Look in its home folder for a dropped note (the flag).

They also left a quiet way back to root: a set-user-ID copy of a shell. find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null lists set-user-ID files; the one with a hidden, odd name under /usr/local/bin is it. Clean up: userdel -r {{ROGUE}} and rm -f /usr/local/bin/{{BDNAME}}.
